section_summary: This section traces U.S. diplomatic and naval-intelligence concern about Japanese activity in Ecuador from 1932 through 1938. Early reports cover Japanese residents and immigrants, alleged charting and fishing around the Galápagos Islands, threats against a proposed fishing concession, and unconfirmed sightings of submarines and a mother ship near the archipelago. The later pages document Japanese propaganda distributed in Guayaquil and reproduce two pamphlets defending Japanese policy in China, including a lengthy account of the opening phase of the Second Sino-Japanese War.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 139: Activities of Japanese Subjects in Ecuador
subfiles.from: Francis White, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Instructs the Quito legation to report information about Japanese activities in Ecuador.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards a copy of a February 6, 1932 despatch from the ambassador at Lima concerning Japanese activities in Peru. Because the Director of Naval Intelligence is interested, Dawson is directed to transmit any similar information that reaches the legation in Ecuador.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 569: Activities of Japanese
subfiles.from: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Reports that no suspicious Japanese activity had been found in Ecuador.
subfiles.summary: Dawson states that discreet inquiries, assisted by the Consulate General at Guayaquil, revealed no activities comparable to those reported from Peru. The legation knew of only one Japanese subject, a cook and small restaurant operator at Santa Elena, and noted that Japan was represented by honorary consul Pedro V. Miller Gutiérrez.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 569 to the Navy Department
subfiles.from: Francis White, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards the Quito legation’s report on Japanese subjects in Ecuador to naval intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends the Navy a copy of William Dawson’s May 4 despatch. The covering letter identifies the report as information requested by the Director of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 586: Activities of Japanese
subfiles.from: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival at Guayaquil of three Japanese agricultural immigrants from Peru.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul Gannett reported that Tokuso Aguena, Masaharu Awakon and Chosho Teugazan entered Ecuador at Guayaquil on May 8 after arriving from Trujillo. All three were Okinawan farmers, and the legation asked Gannett to continue reporting on Japanese arrivals and activities.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1175: Japanese Vessels in the Vicinity of the Galápagos Islands
subfiles.from: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Forwards a report that two Japanese vessels were charting waters around the Galápagos Islands.
subfiles.summary: Dawson encloses an October 17 letter from Consul General Harold B. Quarton in Guayaquil. Quarton’s information, obtained from physician Herman B. Parker, alleged that two Japanese vessels had cruised near the Galápagos, charted surrounding waters and been ordered away by local authorities.

subfiles.title: Letter Reporting an Intercepted Message about Japanese Ships near the Galápagos
subfiles.from: Harold B. Quarton, Consul General at Guayaquil
subfiles.to: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Relays a radio message intercepted by Herman B. Parker about two Japanese ships near the Galápagos.
subfiles.summary: Parker reported intercepting a message that two purported fishing ships spent two weeks charting Galápagos waters before the governor ordered them to leave. Quarton encouraged Parker to share notable intercepts but considered him excitable and possibly biased, and therefore declined to support his wish to become an official Canal Zone secret-service reporter.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Despatch No. 1175 on Japanese Vessels near the Galápagos
subfiles.from: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the report forwarding information on two Japanese vessels near the Galápagos.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Dawson’s account of Harold B. Quarton’s information from Herman B. Parker. It again states that two Japanese vessels allegedly charted Galápagos waters and were ordered away by local authorities.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Letter on Parker’s Intercepted Galápagos Message
subfiles.from: Harold B. Quarton, Consul General at Guayaquil
subfiles.to: William Dawson, American Minister at Quito
subfiles.about: Duplicate of Quarton’s letter concerning an intercepted report of Japanese reconnaissance near the Galápagos.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats Parker’s claim that purported Japanese fishing ships were charting the archipelago. It also repeats Quarton’s reservations about Parker’s reliability and his refusal to seek an official intelligence appointment for him.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Phillips Lord’s Message on Japanese Fishing Boats at Isabela
subfiles.from: State Department
subfiles.about: Points to a message from Phillips Lord to the President concerning Japanese fishing boats visiting Isabela.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs researchers to another file for the underlying message. Its subject entry identifies a report from Phillips Lord to the President about Japanese fishing boats at Isabela in the Galápagos.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Galápagos Fishing Rights and Japanese Espionage
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Assesses allegations that Japanese interests obstructed a non-Japanese Galápagos fishing concession.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum considers the allegation important because the Galápagos lie about 750 miles from the Panama Canal, while acknowledging that it may not be true. It connects the report with other alleged Japanese subversion and espionage, including an incident at Singapore, and concludes that Japanese nationals were systematically advancing Japan’s strategic position.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Galápagos Fishing Rights
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Duplicate assessment of alleged Japanese obstruction of a Galápagos fishing concession.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the Far Eastern Affairs division’s caution that the allegation may be untrue. It nevertheless treats the report as consistent with broader suspicions of organized Japanese espionage and strategic activity.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Commander Holmes concerning Countess Hamon
subfiles.from: J. F. McGurk, Division of Latin-American Affairs
subfiles.about: Records naval intelligence material concerning threats against Countess Hamon’s proposed Galápagos fishing concession.
subfiles.summary: Commander Holmes supplied correspondence about Countess Hamon and her husband, British subjects seeking a Galápagos fishing concession. She claimed that a Japanese man threatened her in Panama and that an anonymous caller repeated the warning in Guayaquil, after which she abandoned her trip to Quito. McGurk found the account fantastic and noted that Hamon also hoped to obtain financial backing from the Secretary of the Navy.

subfiles.title: Mena Hamon’s Letter to Secretary of the Navy Claude Swanson
subfiles.from: Mena Hamon
subfiles.to: Claude Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Requests an interview about Japanese fishing activity and alleged threats connected with her Galápagos concession.
subfiles.summary: Hamon describes traveling from San Pedro through Cristóbal to Guayaquil to complete an Ecuadorian concession for Galápagos fishing rights. She says a Japanese man at the Hotel Washington warned her not to negotiate with President Velasco Ibarra, and that further warnings followed at Guayaquil and aboard the Pacific Grove. She portrays Japanese dominance of fishing as a strategic danger near the Panama Canal and offers additional information in a private interview.

subfiles.title: Grayson’s Preliminary Report on the Hamons
subfiles.from: Grayson, Eleventh Naval District
subfiles.about: Provides an initial background inquiry into Count and Countess Hamon before a personal interview.
subfiles.summary: The investigator reports that the Hamons lived quietly in a secluded Hollywood house and had good reputations. Count Hamon was described as an Irish-born author and lecturer on occult sciences who had lived in London, come to the United States in 1929 and traveled extensively. Grayson planned to interview the couple personally the following day.

subfiles.title: Grayson’s Confidential Interview Report on the Hamons and the Galápagos Concession
subfiles.from: Grayson, Eleventh Naval District
subfiles.about: Reports a detailed interview with the Hamons about their fishing process, concession and alleged Japanese intimidation.
subfiles.summary: The Hamons described Mena Hamon’s fish-dehydration process and correspondence with Ecuadorian officials concerning an exclusive Galápagos fishing concession. She repeated claims of threats in Cristóbal, Guayaquil and aboard ship, accused V. M. Egas and Sam Hornstein of serving Japanese interests, and claimed that dozens of Japanese fishing boats were regularly in the islands. Grayson found the couple credible, considered the concession potentially useful for reducing a perceived threat to the Panama Canal, obtained their correspondence and initiated further inquiries into Egas.

subfiles.title: Navy Department Reply to Countess Hamon
subfiles.from: Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Declines both an immediate Washington interview and Navy financial support for Hamon’s fishing project.
subfiles.summary: The Navy thanks Hamon for her information but says an expensive special trip to Washington is unnecessary because an Eleventh Naval District officer has already contacted her. It also states that the Navy Department cannot provide financial backing, while leaving open the possibility of seeing her if she happens to visit Washington.

subfiles.title: Letter to the Naval Attaché on Reported Submarines in the Galápagos
subfiles.from: Dayle C. McDonough, American Consul General at Guayaquil
subfiles.to: G. L. Weyler, U.S. Naval Attaché at Lima
subfiles.about: Reports local evidence and speculation concerning submarines and a mother ship in Galápagos waters.
subfiles.summary: McDonough encloses an El Universo clipping and reports that employees of the Sociedad Continental believed several small submarines and a mother ship near San Cristóbal were Japanese, partly because of their radio traffic. Ecuador lacked a functioning vessel capable of investigating, while informants distinguished ordinary American fishing activity from allegedly suspicious Japanese operations. McDonough acknowledges that the vessels’ nationality was unproved but promises additional reporting.

subfiles.title: El Universo Clipping: Submarines Seen in the Galápagos
subfiles.from: El Universo and United Press correspondents
subfiles.about: Reports unidentified submarines conducting possible hydrographic or strategic surveys around San Cristóbal, Santa Fé and Española.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says a flotilla accompanied by a warship was seen maneuvering around the eastern Galápagos and may have been studying currents, depths and strategic conditions. Ecuador’s small local garrison and sailing boat could not investigate effectively. Reports from Balboa, Washington and Valparaíso denied that the submarines were American or Chilean, while local observers suspected they were Japanese.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 269 on Japanese Interest in the Galápagos
subfiles.from: Sparks, Ecuador
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch stating that Japanese interests wished to control the Galápagos in an emergency.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers researchers to file 622.9415/10 and Despatch No. 269. Its subject notation says there was a general conviction that Japan desired control of the Galápagos Islands in the event of an emergency.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Cross-reference to Despatch No. 269
subfiles.from: Sparks, Ecuador
subfiles.about: Duplicate reference to the despatch on a purported Japanese desire to control the Galápagos.
subfiles.summary: This sheet duplicates the preceding cross-reference to file 622.9415/10. It again summarizes the referenced despatch as expressing a general belief that Japan sought emergency control of the Galápagos.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 643: Japanese Propaganda in Ecuador
subfiles.from: Dayle C. McDonough, American Consul General at Guayaquil
subfiles.about: Reports distribution in Ecuador of English- and Spanish-language pamphlets defending Japanese policy in China.
subfiles.summary: McDonough says Japanese propaganda in Ecuador had become slightly more active but remained neither intense nor effective. He identifies the English pamphlet “How the North China Affair Arose” and the Lima-printed Spanish pamphlet “El Comunismo en Oriente,” distributed by the Ecuadorian serving as Japanese consul in Guayaquil. The Spanish text rejects multilateral intervention, demands major Chinese political and military concessions and depicts Japan’s war as an anti-Bolshevik crusade.

subfiles.title: El Comunismo en Oriente
subfiles.from: Peru Jiho and Lima Nippo
subfiles.about: Presents a Japanese justification of the conflict with China as an anti-communist campaign.
subfiles.summary: The surviving enclosure includes the title material and concluding argument of a Lima-published pamphlet on the origins, causes and consequences of the Sino-Japanese conflict. It rejects action by the League of Nations and Nine-Power Conference and advocates direct Sino-Japanese negotiations based on Chinese disarmament, recognition of Manchukuo, suppression of anti-Japanese propaganda and removal of Soviet influence. It concludes by portraying Japan as defending peace and civilization in East Asia from Bolshevism.

subfiles.title: How the North China Affair Arose
subfiles.from: Foreign Affairs Association of Japan
subfiles.about: Defends Japanese military action in North China and assigns responsibility for escalation to Chinese forces and the Nanjing government.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet begins with photographs and an account of the foreign military presence in China, then gives a strongly pro-Japanese narrative of the July 1937 clash at Lugou Bridge and subsequent negotiations. It portrays Japanese forces as restrained and defensive, repeatedly accuses the Chinese 29th Army and Nanjing government of breaking agreements, and describes the fighting at Langfang, Guang'anmen, Beijing and Tianjin. The text proceeds to Japanese operations against Chinese forces and begins an account of the Tongzhou massacre; the pamphlet continues beyond page 73.
